description.sr_latin: Fraze za slavlja, zdravice, rođendane, slavu i druženje.
description.en: Phrases for celebrations, toasts, birthdays, slava, and gathering culture.

phrases.context: Everyone's glass is raised around the table and you're all about to clink — give the toast.
phrases.notes: Literally 'may we live' — an imperative-style wish. Hold eye contact as you clink; skipping it reads as rude.

phrases.context: Glasses are up and you want to toast to everyone's good health rather than just clink and drink.
phrases.notes: 'U zdravlje' = to health, with 'zdravlje' in the accusative after 'u'. Personalize it: 'U tvoje zdravlje!' = to your health.

phrases.context: The person next to you sneezes mid-conversation — give the little blessing that doubles as a toast.
phrases.notes: 'Na zdravlje' covers both 'bless you' after a sneeze and 'to your health' over a drink; tone and setting decide which.

phrases.context: It's just you and your partner on a date, glasses raised — make the toast about the two of you.
phrases.notes: 'Za' takes the accusative, so 'mi' becomes 'nas'. A short, warm toast couples make all the time.

phrases.context: You walk in on your friend's big day and hand over their gift — say the standard greeting first.
phrases.notes: 'Srećan' = happy/fortunate (masculine, matching 'rođendan'). 'Rođendan' is literally 'birth-day', from 'roditi' = to be born.

phrases.context: You've just wished a happy birthday and want a warm second line — wish them everything good.
phrases.notes: 'Najbolje' = the best, the superlative of 'dobro'. A go-to add-on after any congratulation or wish.

phrases.context: Glasses go up for the birthday guy and you cheer the wish straight at him alone.
phrases.notes: An old past-tense form used as a cheer: 'Živeo!' to a man, 'Živela!' to a woman, 'Živeli!' to a group.

phrases.context: Your friend is blowing out candles and you want to know the exact age they're hitting this year.
phrases.notes: 'Puniti godine' = to turn an age (literally 'to fill years'); 'godina' is genitive plural after 'koliko'. Warmer than 'Koliko imaš godina?' on a birthday.

phrases.context: You step through the door at a family's patron-saint feast — greet your hosts as you arrive.
phrases.notes: 'Srećna' is feminine, matching 'slava'. Slava is a uniquely Serbian, UNESCO-protected tradition where each family honors its patron saint yearly.

phrases.sr_latin: Da Bog da slavili još mnogo godina!
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Да Бог да славили још много година!
phrases.en: May you celebrate for many more years!
phrases.context: You're raising a glass at someone's slava and want to give the older, traditional blessing for the day.
phrases.notes: 'Da Bog da' = God willing / may God grant, a fixed blessing frame. 'Godina' is genitive plural after 'mnogo'.

phrases.context: You're getting to know a Serbian friend and want to ask which day their family marks each year.
phrases.notes: The 'ti' is dative — literally 'when is the slava to you'. Asking it lands as genuine interest in the tradition.

phrases.en: Which saint is your family's slava?
phrases.context: You know a family keeps a slava and want to ask which saint they honor, the way you'd ask the whole household.
phrases.notes: 'Vaša' is the formal/plural 'your' because it's the whole family's tradition. Common ones: Sveti Nikola, Sveti Sava, Sveti Đorđe.

phrases.context: The clock strikes midnight on December 31st and you turn to the people around you with the wish.
phrases.notes: 'Srećna' and 'Nova' are both feminine, matching 'godina'. Serbs mark Jan 1 and again Jan 14, the Orthodox 'Srpska Nova godina'.

phrases.context: It's Orthodox Christmas morning, January 7th, and you greet a Serbian friend with the traditional line.
phrases.notes: 'Rodi se' uses an old aorist — 'was born'. Even non-religious Serbs say it; the set reply is 'Vaistinu se rodi!' = indeed He is born.

phrases.context: You're heading out before the holiday break and want to wish coworkers well without naming one specific day.
phrases.notes: 'Praznici' is the plural of 'praznik' = holiday; 'Srećni' agrees in the masculine plural. A safe catch-all around the season.

phrases.context: Everyone's glass is empty and the night is still young — push the table for another round.
phrases.notes: 'Ajmo' is colloquial for 'hajdemo' = let's go. 'Jednu' is accusative feminine, agreeing with an unspoken 'čašu' = glass.

phrases.en: Nothing's gonna happen to you, drink!
phrases.context: You're trying to slow down and your Serbian friends won't let you — they wave off your worry, affectionately.
phrases.notes: 'Neće biti' is the negated future = won't happen; 'ti' is the dative experiencer. 'Pij' = drink (imperative) — the classic nudge.

phrases.sr_latin: Dosta mi je, ne mogu više.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Доста ми је, не могу више.
phrases.en: I've had enough, I can't anymore.
phrases.context: You've reached your limit at the table and want to bow out of the next pour, gently but clearly.
phrases.notes: 'Dosta mi je' = it's enough for me, with 'mi' in the dative. Brace for 'Ma daj, još jednu!' = come on, one more.

phrases.context: Your host is pouring the family brandy and you want to praise it as the homemade pride it clearly is.
phrases.notes: 'Domaća' = homemade (feminine, matching 'rakija'). Homemade rakija is family pride — always compliment it. 'Rakija' comes from Turkish 'rakı'.

phrases.context: Your guests are on the doorstep and you swing the door open — greet them as they step inside.
phrases.notes: Literally 'well come' — 'došli' is a past participle, so it agrees with who arrives: 'došao' (m), 'došla' (f), 'došli' (group).

phrases.en: Take your shoes off, go ahead.
phrases.context: A guest hovers at your hallway unsure what to do — tell them to slip off their shoes and relax.
phrases.notes: 'Izuti se' = to take one's shoes off (imperative 'izuj'); 'slobodno' = feel free. Expect house slippers ('papuče') waiting for you.

phrases.sr_latin: Jesi gladan? Imam da ti ponudim nešto.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Јеси гладан? Имам да ти понудим нешто.
phrases.en: Are you hungry? I've got something to offer you.
phrases.context: A guy just sat down at your place and you, like any Serbian host, immediately want to feed him.
phrases.notes: 'Gladan' is masculine here; say 'gladna?' to a woman. Refusing a Serbian host's food is nearly impossible.

variations.sr_latin: Jesi gladna? Imam da ti ponudim nešto.
variations.sr_cyrillic: Јеси гладна? Имам да ти понудим нешто.
variations.en: Are you hungry? I've got something to offer you.

phrases.context: A guest is sitting stiffly on the edge of your couch — put them at ease in your space.
phrases.notes: 'Kod kuće' = at home, with 'kuće' in the genitive after 'kod'. 'Osećaj se' is the reflexive imperative 'feel yourself'.

phrases.context: The group chat is buzzing about going out and you want to find out where everyone's landing.
phrases.notes: 'Žurka' = party, the everyday informal word. 'Večeras' = tonight, distinct from 'veče' = evening.

phrases.context: It's getting late at the party and you lean over to a friend to gauge how much longer this runs.
phrases.notes: 'Do kad' = until when, with 'kad' a clipped 'kada'. 'Ostajemo' = we stay; the honest answer is usually 'do jutra' = till morning.

phrases.context: The track at the gathering hits and you turn to the host to praise their taste in tunes.
phrases.notes: 'Odlična' is feminine, matching 'muzika'. A quick, natural compliment that always lands well at a party.

phrases.context: The energy is climbing and the song deserves more volume — call out to whoever's on the speaker.
phrases.notes: 'Pojačaj' = turn up (imperative); 'muziku' is accusative as the object. The opposite is 'Smanji muziku' = turn it down.

phrases.context: The night needs somewhere to land and you spontaneously offer up your apartment to the whole crew.
phrases.notes: 'Kod mene' = at my place, with 'mene' in the genitive after 'kod'. This off-the-cuff invite is how most plans actually happen.

phrases.sr_latin: Dolazi, nemoj da se praviš važan.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Долази, немој да се правиш важан.
phrases.en: Come on, don't act all important.
phrases.context: A friend is making excuses to skip out and you push back, ribbing him to stop the fuss and just come.
phrases.notes: 'Praviti se važan' = to act important/aloof; say 'važna' to a woman. A classic, affectionate guilt-trip between friends.

variations.sr_latin: Dolazi, nemoj da se praviš važna.
variations.sr_cyrillic: Долази, немој да се правиш важна.
variations.en: Come on, don't act all important.

phrases.context: You're sorting out a potluck-style gathering and want everyone to claim what they'll carry over.
phrases.notes: 'Donositi' = to bring (imperfective). Typical replies: 'Ja donosim piće' = I'll bring drinks, or 'Ja donosim meze' = I'll bring snacks.

phrases.en: No worries, come whenever you can.
phrases.context: Friends are stressing about being late to your gathering — wave it off and tell them to come at their own pace.
phrases.notes: 'Nema frke' = no stress (slang), with 'frke' genitive after 'nema'. 'Kad stignete' = whenever you manage to make it.

phrases.context: Your friend just told you they passed their driving test — give them the quick, all-purpose congrats.
phrases.notes: 'Čestitati' = to congratulate; 'čestitam' is literally 'I congratulate'. Name the occasion with 'Čestitam ti na...' = congrats on...

phrases.context: A friend just pulled off something genuinely impressive and you want to tip your hat to them.
phrases.notes: Literally 'every honor', with 'svaka' feminine to match 'čast'. Thrown around constantly for wins big and small.

phrases.context: Your partner just shared a real win and you want to tell them, plainly, how proud you feel.
phrases.notes: 'Ponosan' is the masculine speaker form; a woman says 'ponosna'. 'Na tebe' takes the accusative after 'na'.

phrases.context: Your partner announces they landed a raise — react by insisting this absolutely has to be celebrated.
phrases.notes: 'Mora se proslaviti' is an impersonal reflexive = it must be celebrated. Serbs find a reason to celebrate almost anything.

phrases.context: You finally decide to head home and break the news to the whole table that you're leaving.
phrases.notes: 'Moram da idem' = I have to go. Tacking on 'ljudi' = guys/folks keeps the goodbye casual; brace for the long send-off.

phrases.en: Where are you off to? It's early!
phrases.context: Someone at the table just stood up to leave and you protest, insisting the night has barely started.
phrases.notes: 'Gde ćeš' is literally 'where will you', with the future clitic 'ćeš' and the verb left unsaid. The reflex protest when anyone leaves.

phrases.sr_latin: Bilo je odlično, hvala na svemu!
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Било је одлично, хвала на свему!
phrases.en: It was great, thanks for everything!
phrases.context: You've made it to the door at last and turn back to thank your host warmly before stepping out.
phrases.notes: 'Bilo je' = it was (neuter past). 'Hvala na svemu' = thanks for everything, with 'svemu' in the locative after 'na'.

phrases.context: You're parting ways with a friend after a good night and want to leave the door open to meet again.
phrases.notes: 'Vidimo se' = we'll see each other / see you, a reflexive standard for goodbyes. 'Uskoro' = soon.
